identification.summary: NICKEL ALLEY is Sophos Counter Threat Unit's name for a threat group that Sophos describes as operating on behalf of the North Korean government and conducting 'Contagious Interview' activity against technology-sector professionals [S1]. The group often builds a fake LinkedIn company page for credibility and maintains a coordinating GitHub account for malware delivery [S1]. Sophos states that since at least mid-2025 the group has used ClickFix lures to deliver the PyLangGhost RAT [S1]. Sophos also notes that in late 2025 the group established code repositories containing Visual Studio Code 'tasks', and that it conducts opportunistic npm attacks (compromised packages and typosquats) [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Since at least mid-2025 for ClickFix delivery of PyLangGhost, per Sophos [S1]. Earlier start date of NICKEL ALLEY itself not established in sources reviewed.
identification.notes: Sophos's NICKEL ALLEY is tied by Sophos to the Contagious Interview campaign [S1]. Other vendors track Contagious Interview / ClickFake Interview activity under their own names (e.g. Famous Chollima / Wagemole per SOCRadar; Sekoia's ClickFake Interview attributed to Lazarus Group in reporting) [S2][S3]. Cluster boundaries and overlap with NICKEL ALLEY were not verified; do not merge facts across these names.

attribution.basis: Sophos describes NICKEL ALLEY as a threat group operating on behalf of the North Korean government [S1]. The supporting evidence was not available because the full report could not be opened.

objectives: Sophos-derived excerpts indicate targeting of technology professionals via fake job interviews, with malware aimed at exfiltration and profiling [S1]. Malpedia-based summary in the actor record cites focus on Chrome cryptocurrency wallet data, implying theft; this was not independently verified against the full report [S1].

sectors: Cryptocurrency and Web3 (in related Contagious/ClickFake Interview reporting by other vendors, not confirmed for NICKEL ALLEY) [S3]
targeting.notes: Sophos says the group targets professionals in the technology sector via fake job offers [S1]. Regional targeting not established for NICKEL ALLEY; other vendors' reporting on related ClickFake activity mentions crypto/Web3 professionals [S3].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering via fake LinkedIn company pages and a coordinating GitHub account hosting malware [S1]. ClickFix lures in which a fake interview task shows an error and instructs the victim to run a command that starts a chain ending in PyLangGhost RAT [S1]. Late-2025 repositories using Visual Studio Code tasks [S1]. Opportunistic compromise of npm packages and typosquatted npm packages [S1]. PyLangGhost is described by SOCRadar (for Famous Chollima ClickFake activity) as a Python-based Windows RAT, with a macOS counterpart GolangGhost [S3].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: Defense-relevant exposure is personnel and contractors in technology roles who use LinkedIn, GitHub, npm, and developer tooling, including on personal or BYOD devices [S1]. Step 3 (actor): a DPRK-linked group using social engineering, ClickFix, PyLangGhost and VS Code tasks [S1]. MLCOA: continued fake-recruiter outreach with ClickFix or poisoned repositories to developers. MDCOA: supply chain compromise through trojanized or typosquatted npm packages reaching organizational build environments [S1]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited recruiter contact followed by requests to run terminal commands; repositories with .vscode/tasks.json auto-run options; unfamiliar npm packages [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: share the lure pattern (fake interviews, ClickFix commands, VS Code tasks) with developer and contractor populations [S1]. Authorities: monitoring of personal accounts and devices is limited; coordinate through counterintelligence and legal channels. Mission assurance: restrict package installs to vetted registries and review repositories before opening in IDEs with workspace trust [S1]. Coordination: route observations to the supporting cyber threat intelligence cell and vendor/government partners.
